quote: A Bayesian superintelligence, hooked up to a webcam, would invent General Relativity as a hypothesis—perhaps not the dominant hypothesis, compared to Newtonian mechanics, but still a hypothesis under direct consideration—by the time it had seen the third frame of a falling apple. It might guess it from the first frame, if it saw the statics of a bent blade of grass.
content: Three frames of a falling apple contain, at most, a few bits about the dynamics: a position, a velocity, and one estimate of acceleration, and the acceleration is constant to within any webcam’s precision. They say nothing about how the acceleration varies with distance, nothing about the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass, nothing about light, and nothing about curvature, since every distinctively relativistic effect at the surface of the Earth is smaller than the pixel. Solomonoff induction applied to those frames would weight the shortest program consistent with them, which is constant acceleration, and would assign general relativity a weight that is the prior of its much longer program times a likelihood no higher than the constant-acceleration program’s, since both fit the frames equally. That is the mathematics the essay invokes, and it gives the opposite answer. The essay conflates having a hypothesis under consideration (a matter of what mathematics the mind knows; Riemann is the point) with the data supporting it (a matter of information, of which there is almost none). A superintelligence with Riemann’s geometry would list general relativity among a great many alternatives that three frames cannot rank. Einstein needed Mercury; the webcam has less.

quote: Then we cracked their equivalent of the protein folding problem over a century or so, and did some simulated engineering in their simulated physics.
content: The protein folding problem was cracked in our world in the years after this was written, and the way it was cracked bears on the story’s premise. AlphaFold did not solve folding by reasoning from physics on a small amount of data; it learned from roughly 170,000 experimentally determined structures in the Protein Data Bank and from the covariation statistics of millions of sequences (Jumper et al. (2021)), the accumulated output of seventy years of crystallography. The physics-based approach, folding by simulating the energetics, remains far behind for proteins of any size. So the cognitive feat that the story assigns to a fast civilization reading “a tiny handful of physics papers” was, in the one case where it has been done, a feat of data rather than of thought, and the data took a scientific community decades of wet-lab work to produce. The story is a thought experiment about the ratio of intelligence to evidence, and the actual history of the problem it names came down on the side of evidence. Book III’s annotations on The Power of Intelligence found the same pattern for the general claim.
